newsitem.title: USA: Teamsters election official says no ballots missing.
newsitem.headline: Teamsters election official says no ballots missing.

text.p: A court-appointed officer overseeing the Teamsters Union election, under fire from the apparent loser in the race, denied on Friday that ballots were missing and declared her procedures have been sound.

The officer, Barbara Zack Quindel, said double-counting errors by the her staff and the U.S. Postal Service had produced an estimate of mail-in ballots that was more than 25,000 greater than the number actually processed.

"The bottom line here is that there are no missing ballots," Quindel told a telephone news conference. "I am completely satisfied that the procedures that we used in the election guarantee the integrity of the count."

Although a winner for the presidency of the 1.4 million member union has yet to be declared, incumbent president Ron Carey claimed victory last month after interim results showed him with a narrow lead.

His opponent, James Hoffa, son of the late Jimmy Hoffa who ran the union in the 1950s and 1960s, has complained of Quindel's handling of the election and asked Attorney General Janet Reno to impound the ballots and launch an FBI investigation into "serious irregularities." Two lawmakers have also asked Reno to review the election.
U.S. Attorney Mary Jo White responded to Hoffa's request last week, saying the Justice Department and Federal Bureau of Investigation "are closely reviewing and monitoring" the case.

A Justice Department spokesman said a response would be issued next week to House Judiciary Committee Chairman Henry Hyde, R-Ill. and ranking minority member John Conyers, D-Mich., who requested a review of the handling of the election.

Quindel, whose authority to oversee the election was set up under a 1989 settlement of a federal anti-racketeering suit against the union, said the 25,000-ballot discrepancy has been trimmed to slightly more than 2,000 ballots, a statistically insignificant difference of less than 0.5 percent.

Shortly after ballot-counting started on Dec. 10, Quindel reported that postal authorities in the United States and Canada had charged her office for handling 511,268 ballots. But by the end of that week, she was able to account for only 485,604 ballots, a discrepancy of 25,664.
In a review of postal receipts, a double-counting error by one of her staff members was discovered that reduced the postal services' estimates to 502,814, she said.

After an investigation with postal officials, she said several double-counts by the U.S. Postal Service were found that further lowered the total number of ballots for which her office was charged to 487,614, including nearly 20,000 from Canada. Quindel said her office was given a refund for the double counts.

Carey currently leads Hoffa in the balloting by 230,142 to 215,034, with 20,529 so-called challenged ballots still unprocessed and 14,474 others declared ineligible. Quindel said further interim results will be issued on Jan. 7.
